opus-5.5.text:
I think games have been incredibly valuable, and honestly I don't think we'd be where we are today without them. When we started working on things like AlphaGo, AlphaZero and later MuZero, games gave us something that's really hard to find anywhere else: a clean, well-defined environment with a clear objective. You know exactly what winning means, you can simulate as many games as you want, and you can measure progress objectively. You can put your agent against the world champion and see whether it's actually better. That kind of unambiguous feedback loop is incredibly powerful when you're trying to develop new algorithms, because it lets you separate whether an idea doesn't work from whether you just measured it wrong.

Games also let us study really fundamental capabilities in isolation: planning, search, learning from self-play, dealing with huge state spaces. Go was the perfect example. The search space is so vast that brute force doesn't work, so you're forced to develop intuition, essentially learned value functions and policies, combined with search. Many of those ideas, like combining learned models with planning, turned out to be very general.

That said, the limitations are real. The real world doesn't come with a perfect simulator, and it doesn't come with a clean reward function. In Go, the rules are known and fixed. In the real world you have to learn the model of the environment, which is partly why we moved toward MuZero, where the agent learns its own model of the dynamics instead of being given the rules. In the real world you also have partial observability, noise, and very long horizons, and most importantly, it's often unclear what the objective even is. Defining the reward is sometimes the hardest part of the problem.

Another limitation is data. In games you can generate effectively unlimited experience through self-play. In the real world, interactions are expensive, slow, and sometimes unsafe, so you can't just try a hundred million times and learn from your mistakes.

So the way I think about it is that games are a fantastic laboratory. They're where you develop and stress-test the core ideas. But the transition to the real world means relaxing those assumptions one by one: learning the model, learning from limited data, and figuring out what to optimize for. What's exciting now is that with large language models we have a kind of general world knowledge that we never had in the game setting, and combining that with the planning and reinforcement learning techniques we developed in games is, I think, one of the most promising directions in the field.

r002.rationale: It says games rely on known rules and clean objectives, while the real world has partial observability, noise, long horizons, unclear objectives, and limited, costly interactions. This communicates that games cannot capture the real world’s full complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Games have been incredibly useful to us, and I think the reason is that they give you a lot of the properties you want from a research problem without a lot of the noise. You have a clear objective, you can measure progress very precisely, you can generate essentially unlimited experience because the environment is a simulator, and you can run experiments quickly and reproducibly. When we were working on the Atari agents, and later on AlphaGo and AlphaZero, those properties let us iterate on ideas like deep Q-learning or self-play very fast. If something didn't work, you knew within hours or days, not months.

The other thing games give you is a ladder of difficulty. You can start with something simple like Pong and then go to Go, then to StarCraft, which has partial observability, long horizons, and a huge action space. Each step forces you to invent something new. Many of the algorithmic ideas that came out of that, experience replay, Monte Carlo tree search combined with learned value functions, learned models like in MuZero, were not really about the game. They were general ideas that happened to be discovered in a setting where you could actually see them work.

That said, I'm quite honest about the limitations. The biggest one is the reward. In a game someone has designed a scoring function for you. In the real world, specifying what you want is often the hard part, and getting it slightly wrong has consequences. The second is that games are closed worlds. The rules don't change, the state space is well defined, and you can reset. Real environments are open-ended, non-stationary, and you often don't get a second try. A system that has played millions of games of Go has seen the full distribution of what Go can be. A system in the real world is always facing things it hasn't seen.

There's also the question of sample efficiency. AlphaZero played more games than any human could in many lifetimes. That's fine in a simulator, but in robotics or in a scientific lab you simply can't afford that, so a lot of what works in games doesn't transfer until you solve the data problem, either with better priors, better models, or by learning from existing data rather than purely from interaction.

So my view is that games are a very good place to discover and stress-test algorithms, and a bad place to declare victory. Something like AlphaFold is a good example of the right direction, where the search and learning ideas were there, but the actual work was in grounding them in a real domain with real data and real constraints. I think of games as the wind tunnel. You learn a lot about aerodynamics there, but eventually you have to fly the plane.

r002.rationale: It says games are closed worlds while real environments are open-ended and systems continually face situations they have not seen.

astra-6.text:
I think games are very useful because they give you a controlled environment in which you can test ideas. You have clear rules, you can measure how well an agent is doing, and you can generate experience without the cost of making mistakes in the real world. But they can still require quite sophisticated behavior: planning, learning from feedback, and making decisions where the consequences only become apparent much later.

The limitation is that, in a game, somebody has already defined the objective and the boundaries for you. In the real world, it’s often unclear what success means, you don’t observe everything that matters, and you can’t necessarily try something millions of times. So doing well at a game is evidence that an approach can solve certain kinds of problems; it doesn’t establish that it will work everywhere.

For me, the important question is what transfers. Are we developing general methods for learning and decision-making, or are we exploiting something specific to that particular game? Games are a very good place to develop those methods, but ultimately you have to test them beyond games.

r002.rationale: It explains that games have defined objectives and boundaries, while the real world has unclear goals, incomplete observations, and limited opportunities to try things—communicating that games cannot fully represent real-world complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think games are a very useful testbed because they allow us to study intelligence in a setting where we can run experiments quickly and measure progress quite precisely. You have clear rules, an objective, and the ability to generate experience. But within that setting, you can still face very difficult problems: planning over long horizons, learning from delayed rewards, and deciding which possibilities are worth exploring.

The limitation is that the real world doesn’t come with all of those conveniences. Often the objective itself is unclear, you don’t observe the full state of the environment, and you can’t afford to learn by making millions of mistakes. So success in a game doesn’t automatically imply that a system will be useful or reliable outside it.

For me, the important question is whether we’re developing general methods through games, rather than methods that depend on the peculiarities of a particular game. Games can give us evidence that an approach works and help us understand why. Then we need to test which of those ideas survive when we remove the clean rules, the cheap simulation, and the clear reward signal.
